accepted: Vascular dementia: subcortical ischaemic (small-vessel) type, severe, with pseudobulbar affect and spastic gait from bilateral internal capsule lacunes
major neurocognitive disorder due to vascular disease

differential.key_features: Recall benefits from cueing, medial temporal atrophy is age-appropriate, and the pyramidal signs, dysarthria and pseudobulbar affect are not features of Alzheimer's disease
The sudden brief stereotyped weeping with a CNS-LS of 17 and a Geriatric Depression Scale of 3/15 is pseudobulbar affect, a corticobulbar sign, not a mood disorder
Despite the atrial flutter history he has been in documented sinus rhythm for nine years and the imaging shows no cortical or territorial infarct — the burden is entirely small-vessel
Falls, dysarthria and a frontal profile overlap, but there is no vertical gaze palsy, no axial rigidity and no midbrain atrophy, and the lacunar burden explains the picture
No fluctuation, hallucinations, parkinsonism or dream enactment

key_clinical_evidence: Pseudobulbar affect is a tract sign, not a mood disorder: brief stereotyped episodes incongruent with mood, with a CNS-LS above threshold, localise to corticobulbar interruption — here bilateral internal capsule lacunes
An arrhythmia history does not make a dementia cardioembolic: the imaging decides, and here there is no cortical or territorial infarct at all

Deep microbleeds and recurrent falls on apixaban call for modifying bleeding risk (blood pressure, alcohol, falls) rather than stopping an anticoagulant that CHA2DS2-VA still indicates after flutter ablation
Medial temporal atrophy must be read against age: Scheltens 1-2 at 82 is within the normal range and does not indicate Alzheimer pathology
Sparing of the anterior temporal poles and U-fibres argues against hereditary small-vessel disease in a patient of this age

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Giorgio Panetta is an 82-year-old retired print-works foreman who lives alone and attends with his niece. Over four years he has become progressively slower, quieter and less capable: he no longer cooks, has stopped paying his own bills after two missed rent payments, and cannot use the telephone menu at the bank. His niece describes an unusual symptom that troubles him most: he weeps suddenly and briefly, several times a week, at things that do not sadden him — a television advertisement, a greeting — and stops as abruptly. He denies feeling depressed and is embarrassed by the episodes. His memory, in her account, is 'patchy but promptable'. His speech has become strained and hard to follow on the telephone. He has fallen twice in six months on the stairs of his building and now uses a stick. There have been no discrete episodes of weakness, and no visual hallucinations, fluctuation in alertness or dream enactment. His atrial flutter was ablated nine years ago, he has been in documented sinus rhythm on annual ECGs since, and he has nonetheless remained on apixaban. His blood pressure has been in the 150-170 range for years.
